q: Margaret River's signature white blends two Bordeaux grapes, often with a little oak, and appears on so many lists that it is written as three letters. Which two grapes?
exp: The blend pairs Sauvignon Blanc's aromatic lift with Semillon's weight and its willingness to take oak, and neither grape gives the same wine alone. It is a direct import from white Bordeaux, adapted to a far sunnier place.

q: Vintages in Margaret River vary far less than in Bordeaux, and a poor year there is rarely a washout. What makes the season so even?
opts: Elevation above six hundred metres keeps every night uniformly cold
A rain shadow removes almost all of the winter rainfall
Persistent summer cloud screens the vineyards from the sun
Ocean on three sides holds the temperature inside a narrow band all season
exp: A large body of water changes temperature slowly, so a maritime climate has small daily and seasonal swings. The rain also falls mainly in winter, well clear of flowering and harvest, which removes the two moments at which a European vintage is usually lost.

q: Western Australia's biggest region by area spreads inland and along the south coast, and divides into five named subregions including Frankland River and Porongurup. Which region?
exp: Great Southern also contains Mount Barker, Albany and Denmark, and the five differ enough that many labels name the subregion rather than the region. Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are all made well there, which is unusual inside one name.

q: Of the five Great Southern subregions, one lies furthest inland along a river, runs warmest and driest, and is planted heavily to Shiraz and Cabernet. Which?
exp: Distance from the coast makes Frankland River the most continental of the five, with warmer days, colder nights and less rain. Albany and Denmark sit on the water, and their cooler, wetter conditions push them toward Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

q: An island lying between forty-one and forty-three degrees south grows much of the fruit behind Australia's finest traditional-method sparkling wine. Which state?
exp: Tasmania is cold enough that Chardonnay and Pinot Noir reach flavour ripeness at low sugar and very high acidity, which is precisely what a sparkling base needs. The conditions that make still wine a gamble there make the bubbles dependable.

q: Tamar Valley, Pipers River and Coal River Valley all appear on Tasmanian labels, yet not one of them is a Geographical Indication. What is registered instead?
opts: The whole island, as a single Geographical Indication
Nothing at all: Tasmania has no Geographical Indication
Only the northern half of the island
Each of the three, but as zones rather than as regions
exp: Tasmania is one GI covering the entire state, with no official regions or subregions inside it, so those area names are informal usage. Given how differently the north coast and the drier south-east ripen, a single name conceals a great deal of variation.

q: Tasmania's most planted variety gives a still red that is pale to medium in colour, red-fruited and high in acid. Which variety?
exp: Pinot Noir serves two purposes on the island: it is the backbone of the sparkling wine and it makes the most convincing still red. Cabernet is planted only in the warmest pockets and fails to ripen in most years.

q: Almost all Tasmanian vineyards sit along the north coast or down the eastern side, and the west carries none. What rules the west out?
opts: It takes the full force of the westerlies and their rainfall
It has no soil anywhere deep enough to plant
It is far too warm and dry for anything but table grapes
exp: The Roaring Forties cross thousands of kilometres of open ocean and strike the west coast first, dumping several times the rain that falls on Hobart. The eastern side lies in the rain shadow of the central highlands, and that is where the vines are.

q: Australia's most widely planted variety carries one name here and a different one in the Rhone valley it came from. What is the Rhone name?
exp: Shiraz and Syrah are one grape, and the two words now signal a difference in expectation rather than in genetics: Shiraz suggests ripeness and sweetness of fruit, Syrah restraint and pepper. Many Australian producers choose between them deliberately to flag which style is in the bottle.

q: Mataro appears on Australian labels for a black grape the rest of the world knows by two other names. Which two?
exp: Mourvedre is the French name and Monastrell the Spanish, while Mataro travelled to Australia with early cuttings and stuck. It ripens very late and gives dark, meaty, firmly tannic wine, which is why it usually turns up as the M in a blend rather than on its own.

q: Blending Shiraz from three separate regions before bottling is treated in Australia as a craft rather than as a compromise. What does the practice buy the winemaker?
opts: Components with different strengths, which hold a house style steady
Exemption from auditing of the label's claims
A legal requirement that applies above a certain alcohol level
The right to print any regional name on the label
exp: One region brings colour and tannin, another perfume, another acidity, and no single site delivers all of them every season. The trade is that no one region can be named alone unless it supplies at least eighty-five percent of the wine. The label must otherwise list the regions in descending order with their percentages, or fall back on a broad Geographical Indication such as South Eastern Australia.

q: A fortified wine from north-east Victoria was called Tokay until an agreement with the European Union obliged Australia to surrender the name. What is it called now, and what is it made from?
opts: Muscat, from Muscat a Petits Grains
exp: Muscadelle is a Bordeaux grape with no fortified tradition at home, and in Rutherglen it gives cold tea, malt and butterscotch, quite distinct from the raisiny Muscat made alongside it. Apera and Tawny are the replacement names Australia adopted for its sherry and port styles under the same agreement.

q: Poured cool with turkey at a midsummer Christmas, a dark foaming full-bodied red just off dry has been an Australian fixture since the nineteenth century. What is it?
opts: A sweet red made in the Lambrusco manner
exp: The style began in Victoria's Great Western and survives almost nowhere else on earth. A full red base takes a second fermentation for pressure, and the dosage leaves just enough sugar to carry the tannin, which is why it is served cool rather than cellar-warm.

q: Draw a line down the middle of Austria and almost no commercial vineyard falls on the western side of it. What accounts for that?
opts: Planting rights are issued only to the eastern federal states
The Danube runs only through the eastern half of the country
The vines start east of the Alps, where the land falls away
The western half is too wet and too warm for any classic variety
exp: All four wine states sit east or south-east of the Alps, where the land drops and the growing season lengthens. West of that line the ground is high, cold and steep, and the few vines there are a curiosity rather than a trade.

q: Terraced vineyards follow a river that enters Lower Austria from the west, passes Krems and Vienna and leaves for Slovakia. Which river, and what does it give the slopes above it?
opts: The Danube, which moderates temperature and bounces light back
The Inn, which carries cold Alpine meltwater past the vineyards
The March, which marks the Czech border in the north
The Mur, which drains the southern Styrian hills
exp: A large body of moving water warms slowly and cools slowly, so the Danube blunts spring frost and holds warmth into the autumn, and its surface bounces light back up onto the terraces above it. The Inn and the Mur are Alpine rivers well away from the classic vineyards, and the March forms the eastern border with Slovakia rather than the northern one.

q: At roughly forty-seven to forty-eight degrees north, Austrian vineyards share a latitude band with which French wine region?
exp: Chablis sits within half a degree of Vienna and the Cote d'Or a little over a degree further south, which is part of why Austrian growers watch Burgundy so closely. Bordeaux and the Languedoc are considerably further south, and Champagne sits a degree or more north again.
